lessons.title: Case Study: Working Out HRA for a Bengaluru Techie Who Moves Cities Mid-Year

body.text: One employee, one tax year, and almost every rule in this course: a rent above the TDS threshold, an appraisal, a transfer from a 50% city to a 40% city, a home loan on a flat in another town, an employer that got the calculation wrong, and a regime choice that turns on a few thousand rupees.

children.text: Arjun Rao is a software engineer at a product company in Bengaluru. His tax year 2026-27 looks messy on paper, which makes it perfect for a final walkthrough. We will work out his exemption period by period, see where his employer went wrong, fix it in his return, and check whether the old regime was worth it at all.

Other facts. His gross salary for the year is ₹22,60,000, including special allowance. He owns a flat in Mysuru where his parents live, with a home loan on which he pays ₹2,45,000 of interest. His PF and other investments fill the ₹1,50,000 limit under Section 123 (80C), he pays ₹25,000 for health insurance and puts ₹50,000 into NPS. He has declared the old regime to his employer. His Bengaluru landlord and his Coimbatore landlord both have valid PANs.

body.text: Before reading on, try it yourself. Split his year into three periods, work out the three limits for each, and add them up. The answer is below, and the periods are the only tricky part.

children.text: Step 1: The Exemption, Period by Period

Look at what changed. In Bengaluru his high rent left Limit 2 comfortably above his HRA, so his exemption was capped by how much HRA he received and by 50% of salary. In Coimbatore, on a much lower rent and a 40% city, Limit 2 collapsed to ₹37,500 and became the binding limit. Five months of the year contribute only ₹37,500 of exemption.
Step 2: Where His Employer Went Wrong

Arjun updated his rent in the HR portal when he moved, but his payroll team calculated the exemption on annual totals: total HRA, total rent, and Bengaluru at 50% for the whole year. That is the pooling error from Lesson 8.

body.text: An overstated exemption is not a windfall. Arjun's Form 130 shows ₹4,60,000, so his TDS was ₹26,520 too low. If he simply copies Form 130 into his return, he under-reports his income. The fix is to claim the correct ₹3,75,000 and pay the difference, which is exactly what an honest return looks like when payroll gets it wrong in your favour.

children.text: Step 3: TDS on the Bengaluru Rent
His Bengaluru rent of ₹70,000 a month crossed ₹50,000, so Section 393(1) applied. He vacated at the end of October, which makes October the last month of that tenancy.

events.title: Deduct 2% from the last rent
events.description: Rent paid to that landlord for the year was ₹4,90,000 over 7 months. TDS at 2% is ₹9,800, deducted from the October rent.

events.title: File Form 141 and deposit
events.description: PAN-based challan-cum-statement, no TAN needed, within 30 days from the end of October.

events.title: Issue Form 132
events.description: The TDS certificate for his Bengaluru landlord, within 15 days of the Form 141 due date.

events.title: No TDS in Coimbatore
events.description: Rent of ₹18,000 a month is below the ₹50,000 threshold, so no deduction is needed.

body.text: The Form 141 acknowledgement is also evidence. It records both PANs and the rent paid, and the credit appears in his landlord's AIS. For the months it covers, Arjun has government-held proof that the rent was real.

children.text: Step 4: The Return, and the Regime Question

body.caption: Three versions of the same year

stats.label: Extra tax to pay at filing

children.text: Even after correcting the exemption downwards, the old regime still wins for Arjun, by ₹11,180. The reason is the combination: ₹3,75,000 of HRA, ₹2,00,000 of home loan interest and ₹2,25,000 of other deductions. Take away the home loan and the new regime would be ahead. This is the pattern from Lesson 10, and it is why he should redo this comparison every year, especially now that five months of his year are spent in a 40% city on low rent.

Old regime, correct claim: ₹22,60,000 minus ₹50,000 standard deduction, ₹3,75,000 exempt HRA, ₹2,00,000 interest and ₹2,25,000 of deductions gives taxable income of ₹14,10,000. Tax is ₹1,12,500 on the first ₹10,00,000 plus 30% of ₹4,10,000, which is ₹1,23,000, totalling ₹2,35,500 before cess and ₹2,44,920 after 4% cess.

New regime: ₹22,60,000 minus ₹75,000 gives ₹21,85,000. Tax across the slabs is ₹2,46,250 before cess and ₹2,56,100 after. The difference of ₹11,180 is what his HRA, home loan and deductions are worth to him this year.

cells: Keep both rent agreements, receipts and bank statements in one folder
Two landlords and two cities mean two evidence sets
File Form 141 and issue Form 132 for the Bengaluru rent
Avoids interest and late fees, and creates independent proof
Tell payroll the calculation must be split at August and November
As soon as he sees Form 130
A corrected Form 130 keeps his return and his employer record consistent
Before the due date, generally 31 July 2027
Claiming the employer figure would be under-reporting
Interest may apply if the shortfall was large enough to require advance tax
Compare both regimes with the corrected figures
The gap is only ₹11,180, so it can flip next year

body.title: Try It: If He Had Not Moved
body.prompt: Suppose Arjun stayed in Bengaluru for the whole year at ₹70,000 a month, with basic ₹90,000 and HRA ₹45,000 for April to July and basic ₹1,05,000 and HRA ₹52,500 from August to March. What would his total exempt HRA be? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: April to July: salary ₹3,60,000, HRA ₹1,80,000, rent ₹2,80,000. Limit 2 is ₹2,44,000 and Limits 1 and 3 are ₹1,80,000, so ₹1,80,000. August to March: salary ₹8,40,000, HRA ₹4,20,000, rent ₹5,60,000. Limit 2 is ₹4,76,000 and Limits 1 and 3 are ₹4,20,000, so ₹4,20,000. Total ₹6,00,000, which is ₹2,25,000 more than his actual ₹3,75,000. The transfer to a 40% city with lower rent cost him most of that.

body.title: Scenario: The Colleague Who Moved the Other Way
body.scenario: Arjun's colleague Divya transferred from Coimbatore to Bengaluru on 1 November, the mirror image of his move. Her basic is ₹1,00,000 a month all year and her HRA is ₹50,000. She paid ₹15,000 a month in Coimbatore and ₹60,000 a month in Bengaluru, and she is on the old regime.
body.prompt: Work out her exempt HRA for the year, and say which limit binds in each period.
body.modelAnswer: April to October, Coimbatore, 7 months at 40%: salary ₹7,00,000, HRA ₹3,50,000, rent ₹1,05,000. Limit 1 is ₹3,50,000, Limit 2 is ₹1,05,000 minus ₹70,000 = ₹35,000, Limit 3 is ₹2,80,000. Limit 2 binds, so ₹35,000. November to March, Bengaluru, 5 months at 50%: salary ₹5,00,000, HRA ₹2,50,000, rent ₹3,00,000. Limit 1 is ₹2,50,000, Limit 2 is ₹3,00,000 minus ₹50,000 = ₹2,50,000, Limit 3 is ₹2,50,000. All three are equal at ₹2,50,000, so ₹2,50,000. Her total is ₹2,85,000. Note that her Bengaluru rent of ₹60,000 a month also crosses the TDS threshold, so she must deduct 2% of ₹3,00,000, which is ₹6,000, from her March rent and file Form 141.

body.title: The Course in One Checklist
steps: Confirm you receive HRA, pay rent for a home you do not own, and are on the old regime
Work out salary for HRA: basic plus eligible DA plus turnover commission
Split the year wherever rent, salary, HRA or city changes
For each period, take the smallest of HRA received, rent minus 10% of salary, and 50% or 40% of salary
Pay rent by bank transfer, collect monthly receipts and give landlord PAN above ₹1,00,000 of annual rent
Deduct TDS if rent crosses ₹50,000 a month, or from the first rupee if your landlord is an NRI
Declare rent in Form 124 and submit proofs before your employer's deadline
Compare old and new regime tax, then file your original return by the due date and claim the correct figure, even if Form 130 differs

points: A messy year is just several simple years: split at every change and apply the three limits to each period
Arjun's correct exemption is ₹3,75,000, while pooling the year would have given ₹4,60,000 and under-reported his income
A move from a 50% city with high rent to a 40% city with low rent can cut an exemption sharply, mostly through Limit 2
Employer errors can go either way. Claim the correct figure in your return and pay any shortfall
Rent above ₹50,000 a month brings a TDS duty, which also produces strong evidence for the HRA claim
The regime choice can turn on a few thousand rupees, so redo the comparison every year with your actual figures

body.text: This case study is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or financial advice. Arjun and Divya are fictional, and the figures are simplified: they ignore professional tax, surcharge and any income other than salary. Provisions reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 and the Income-tax Rules, 2026 as understood at the time of writing. Verify current rules or consult a qualified chartered accountant before acting.
